lines.text: In November twenty twenty-six, Amazon warned New York shoppers that a proposed city law, the Delivery Protection Act, could add up to five dollars to every order.

The mayor, Zohran Mamdani, answered on X. "Amazon is a multi-trillion dollar company. If Jeff Bezos adds five dollars to your order, it's not because of City Council's efforts to protect workers' rights and keep our streets safe. It's greed."
Notice the move. New rules about how deliveries must be run cost money to follow. But according to the mayor, the law can't be the reason prices go up. And if they go up anyway, that's greed.
lines.say: [deadpan] Notice the move. New rules about how deliveries must be run cost money to follow. But according to the mayor, the law can't be the reason prices go up. And if they go up anyway, that's greed.

lines.text: Sit with that for a second. If passing on a cost is greed, then not passing it on is generosity. Absorbing a cost you could charge for is giving money away. That's charity, demanded by City Hall.
lines.say: [dryly] Sit with that for a second. If passing on a cost is greed, then not passing it on is generosity. Absorbing a cost you could charge for is giving money away. That's charity, demanded by City Hall.

lines.text: And that's meant literally. Charge a customer five dollars less than you could, or charge full price and mail them a five-dollar check. Run the books both ways, and the company ends the year with exactly the same money, and so does the customer. Economically, it's a donation.
lines.say: [measured] And that's meant literally. Charge a customer five dollars less than you could, or charge full price and mail them a five-dollar check. Run the books both ways, and the company ends the year with exactly the same money, and so does the customer. Economically, it's a donation.

lines.text: And if the point is that Amazon is a multi-trillion dollar company and can afford it, fine. Then tax it, openly, and let voters see the bill. That's a different policy from this one.

And notice who's being drafted to fund it. Not taxpayers in general. Whoever happens to own shares in one particular company. Why them, and not everyone? Hold that question. We'll see the exact same move again, with a landlord.
This is the mayor of the largest city in America. And this is how he thinks about prices.
lines.say: [deadpan] This is the mayor of the largest city in America. And this is how he thinks about prices.

lines.text: Here's the claim this video is going to defend. Nearly every policy on the socialist menu is the same mistake, repeated over and over. Once you see the mistake, you can't unsee it.
But first, a warning, because you're going to think you know where this is going. You probably don't.
When someone attacks socialism, you know the script. Taxes are theft. Handouts make people lazy. Cut the safety net.
That's not the argument we're making.
This video takes no position on how much we should help the poor. More than now, less than now, none at all. That's a question of values, and you're entitled to your own answer.
Our question is narrower, and a lot harder to wriggle out of. Whatever amount of help you've decided on, what's the least wasteful way to deliver it?
If at any point you think you hear the case for cutting welfare, you don't. That's not the argument we're making, and we'll keep saying so.
First, a word on terms, because someone in the comments is already typing.

What is socialism, exactly? Even its founders weren't tidy about it. Marx and Engels used socialism and communism loosely, and over their careers applied both words to their own ideas. The neat version, where socialism is a waystation on the road to communism, came later, mostly from Lenin.

People use the word for everything from Soviet five-year plans to Scandinavian welfare states. So forget the dictionary. Look at what self-described socialists actually run on. Mamdani's platform is a good sample: a rent freeze, city-run grocery stores, fare-free buses, and mandates like the delivery law.
Add the rest of the usual menu. Price controls, like rent control and the minimum wage. Nationalized industries. Benefits handed out in kind instead of in cash.

Underneath every item is the same move: replace a price the market would set with a decision made politically. Rent control is a city official deciding what an apartment is allowed to cost. That's central planning, one building at a time.
The concept is called deadweight loss. The clearest way to see it is a gift.

Say I buy you a sweater for ten dollars. How much is it worth to you? We don't have to guess. Offer you a choice: keep the sweater, or take cash instead. The smallest amount of cash you'd accept in its place is what it's worth to you. Say it's seven dollars. Economists call that revealed preference: your own choice tells us the value.
So I've spent ten dollars, and you've gained something worth seven. The other three dollars just disappeared. I didn't get them. You didn't get them. Nobody did.
lines.say: [calmly] So I've spent ten dollars, and you've gained something worth seven. The other three dollars just disappeared. I didn't get them. You didn't get them. Nobody did.

lines.text: This isn't a thought experiment. The economist Joel Waldfogel asked people what cash they'd have accepted in place of each holiday gift they received, and found that somewhere between a tenth and a third of what givers spent simply evaporated.

To be fair, a holiday gift carries things cash can't: the thought behind it, the ritual, the people around the tree. Nobody's saying you should mail your grandmother a check. But none of that sentiment comes with a housing voucher. You're not sipping eggnog with Uncle Sam.
lines.say: [warmly] To be fair, a holiday gift carries things cash can't: the thought behind it, the ritual, the people around the tree. Nobody's saying you should mail your grandmother a check. But none of that sentiment comes with a housing voucher. You're not sipping eggnog with Uncle Sam.

lines.text: Hand me a ten-dollar bill instead, and nothing is lost. That missing three dollars is deadweight loss. Value that could have existed, and doesn't.
It gets bigger. When two people trade freely, both expect to come out ahead, or they'd walk away.

Economists have a name for a change that makes someone better off and nobody worse off. A Pareto improvement. It's the one kind of change you can call good without weighing one person's happiness against another's.

Every voluntary trade is a little Pareto improvement. Say Dana would fix your roof for twenty dollars an hour, and you'd happily pay twenty-five. The job happens, and five dollars of value appears out of nowhere, split between you.
Now put an eight-dollar tax on that hour of work. Dana needs twenty-eight to make it worthwhile. You'll only pay twenty-five. The job never happens.
The government collects nothing. Dana loses the work. Your roof still leaks. And five dollars of value never comes into existence.
Hold onto those two ideas. Benefits that are worth less than they cost. Taxes that kill trades that would have happened. Those are the two leaks. And the socialist toolkit is built out of them.
Rent control. The flagship. Mamdani campaigned on freezing the rent on a million stabilized apartments.
So take one. Market rent, three thousand dollars a month. Controlled rent, two thousand.
The tenant saves a thousand dollars a month. Where does that thousand come from?
Not from the city. Not from taxpayers. It comes out of one person's pocket: whoever happened to own that particular building.

So rent control is a thousand-dollar housing voucher, funded by a thousand-dollar tax on one landlord, chosen more or less at random. Propose that policy in those words, and almost nobody would vote for it. Rent control is the same policy, under a friendlier name.

And notice what rent control can't live without. If the landlord could simply decline to renew the lease, the discount would vanish at the end of the year. So rent control always comes with eviction control. In New York, a rent-stabilized tenant has a legal right to renew, and the landlord can't end the lease just because the rent is below market. The thousand-dollar tax never expires.
And it gets worse, because people respond.

The tenant's discount only works in this one apartment. So they stay put long after it suits them. The job across town, the bigger place for the new baby, the smaller place after the kids leave. All of it now costs a thousand dollars a month in lost discount.

Landlords respond too. When economists studied rent control in San Francisco, they found landlords cut the supply of rental housing by fifteen percent, by converting buildings to condos and redeveloping them. Which pushed up rents for everyone who didn't already have a controlled unit.
When leading economists were surveyed on whether rent control had made housing more affordable in the cities that tried it, almost none agreed. This is about as close to consensus as economics gets.
So rent control fails both tests. It's a benefit worth less than it costs, and it's a tax that kills trades. A double leak.
Rent control is one example of a pattern so common it deserves a name. Call it the gift card fallacy.

The gift card fallacy is the belief that you help people more by giving them something specific than by giving them money. A food card instead of cash. A housing unit instead of cash. A discount on one thing instead of cash.

Put another way, a benefit in kind is just cash, with a restriction on how you can spend it. Handing you a ten-dollar sweater is the same as handing you ten dollars, plus one rule: you may only spend it on this sweater. And a rule can never give you more options. It can only take them away.
Every gift card is the sweater. The family receives something worth less to them than what it cost to provide. The gap vanishes.

This part isn't a matter of opinion. Give the family the cash instead. If they'd have bought exactly what the gift card buys, the gift card was only as good as cash. If they'd buy something else, then by their own choice, that something else was worth more to them. Either way, cash is at least as good. It is never worse.

Here's a test that makes it concrete. Say you land a rent-stabilized apartment, and you'd rather live somewhere cheaper and keep the difference. So you sublet it at the market rate, move, and spend the extra on food, or childcare, or whatever your family needs most.

That's against the rules. In New York, subletting a rent-stabilized apartment for more than the legal rent, plus a small surcharge if it's furnished, can get you evicted and leave you owing your subtenant up to three times the overcharge. Try it with a public housing unit, and you can lose the unit.

Think about what that means. Refusing to give people cash comes with an enforcement arm. When someone converts their gift card into cash on their own, you punish them for it. The policy only works if you stop people from spending their own benefit the way they think best.
lines.say: [deadpan] Think about what that means. Refusing to give people cash comes with an enforcement arm. When someone converts their gift card into cash on their own, you punish them for it. The policy only works if you stop people from spending their own benefit the way they think best.

lines.text: The usual objection to cash is that the poor will waste it. That's been tested, a lot. A World Bank review of nineteen studies found that when poor families get cash, spending on alcohol and tobacco doesn't go up. If anything, it goes down.
So before we go further, here's the alternative, in four sentences.
Whatever amount of help you want to give, give it as cash. The same check to every citizen.
Pay for it with taxes that don't block useful trades: taxes on pollution, and on the value of land. If that's not enough, one flat tax on spending.
That's it. Same help, far less waste. The rest of this video is about why that works, and why almost every policy you hear called socialist does the opposite.
Now watch how far the pattern goes.

A public housing lottery. Win it, and you get one particular apartment, in one particular building, in one particular neighborhood. Almost certainly not the one you'd have picked if you'd been handed the money. Gift card.

Food stamps. To be fair, for most families they work almost like cash, because most families spend more on groceries than the benefit is worth anyway. The waste comes from the rules, like the ban on hot meals, and only when those rules change what a family actually buys. A partial gift card. Partial credit.

And notice who else adds rules. Starting in twenty twenty-five, the Trump administration approved state after state's request to ban soda and candy from food stamps. Plenty of progressives called that paternalism, and they were right: a benefit with strings attached is worth less to the person getting it. But rent control, city grocery stores and free-but-only-for-this programs are the same move. Help, but only in the form a politician approves.
lines.say: [dryly] And notice who else adds rules. Starting in twenty twenty-five, the Trump administration approved state after state's request to ban soda and candy from food stamps. Plenty of progressives called that paternalism, and they were right: a benefit with strings attached is worth less to the person getting it. But rent control, city grocery stores and free-but-only-for-this programs are the same move. Help, but only in the form a politician approves.

lines.text: Free street parking. Curb space in a city is some of the most valuable land on earth, handed out free to whoever owns a car. Paid for by everyone, including the people who don't. A gift card for drivers.
Price gouging laws. We'll come back to these, because they deserve their own section.

Mamdani's city-owned grocery stores, which wouldn't pay rent or property tax. Those waived costs are a subsidy, delivered only to people who live near one of the stores and want to shop there. Why not give people the money and let them shop wherever they like? Gift card, with a location attached.

Fare-free buses, another Mamdani promise. This one gets partial credit too. Buses take cars off the road, and fewer cars means less traffic and pollution for everyone. That's a real case for subsidizing them. But zero fares go to every rider, rich or poor, and the cleaner fix is charging drivers for the congestion they cause. A gift card with a half-decent excuse.

And the right does this too, by the way. A tariff is a gift card for one domestic industry, paid for by every consumer who buys its products. Studies of the 2018 tariffs found that nearly the whole cost landed on American buyers. Same mistake, different team.
The gift card fallacy isn't unique to socialists. But socialism is the political program built almost entirely out of it.

Which brings us back to Amazon. The Delivery Protection Act is meant to help delivery workers. Fine. But it doesn't hand them money. It loads costs onto every online order in the city, including orders from people poorer than the workers it's meant to help. A hidden sales tax, paid in the dark.
lines.say: [dryly] Which brings us back to Amazon. The Delivery Protection Act is meant to help delivery workers. Fine. But it doesn't hand them money. It loads costs onto every online order in the city, including orders from people poorer than the workers it's meant to help. A hidden sales tax, paid in the dark.

lines.text: Policy after policy, take it apart and you find the same machine inside. Help delivered in kind instead of cash. Paid for by a tax on some trade that would otherwise have happened.
Every time there's a storm, a strike, or a wave of cancelled flights, the same outrage cycle kicks off. Uber triples its prices. Gouging! Greed! Somebody pass a law.
So think about the night the flights get grounded. Thousands of stranded travelers open the app at once. There are only so many cars.
Who should get one? The traveler stuck at the airport at midnight with a sick kid, or the guy running an errand he could just as easily do tomorrow?
You can't tell them apart by looking. Neither can Uber. But the price can. At triple the fare, the errand waits until tomorrow, and the car goes to someone whose trip can't wait.
And the price does something else. It tells the driver who was planning to stay home tonight that tonight is the night to work. A surge rations the cars, and it summons more of them.
Cap the price, and both effects vanish. The cars go to whoever taps first. The extra drivers stay home. The stranded family waits.

Here's the thing nobody says. Surge pricing is just happy hour, viewed from the other direction. Nobody calls it generosity when a bar cuts prices at four in the afternoon. It's the same signal: come now, there's room. Surge pricing says: only come now if it matters, and drivers, please show up.
lines.say: [dryly] Here's the thing nobody says. Surge pricing is just happy hour, viewed from the other direction. Nobody calls it generosity when a bar cuts prices at four in the afternoon. It's the same signal: come now, there's room. Surge pricing says: only come now if it matters, and drivers, please show up.

lines.text: And if what bothers you is that a poor family can't afford the surge, fine. That's a real concern about equity. Which is a case for giving that family more money, every day of the year. Breaking the one signal that gets cars to the people who need them helps nobody.
A price cap is a discount for whoever's quickest, paid for by everyone left stranded. Gift card fallacy. Again.
Now, here's the part where conservatives and libertarians usually take a victory lap. See? Rent control is a disaster. Scrap it. Scrap the minimum wage. Scrap the food stamps.
And replace them with nothing.

That's why their argument never lands. To a voter who wants to help people, "replace it with nothing" sounds exactly like "I don't want to help people." And the socialist on social media gets to say: you think kids shouldn't eat?

Take the minimum wage. The evidence on moderate increases is mixed. Some studies find meaningful job losses. Others find almost none. It's at least plausible that a modest minimum wage helps low earners more than it costs, up to a point.
We're not going to pretend otherwise. If your only choices were a modest minimum wage or nothing, the minimum wage might win.
But those aren't your only choices. That's the whole point.
You'll hear a phrase thrown at anyone who criticizes these policies. Trickle-down economics.

Let's be precise about what it means, because almost nobody is. The trickle-down claim is this: if you remove some distorting tax or subsidy, the economy grows enough that even the people who were being helped come out ahead. The efficiency gain outweighs the lost equity.
Sometimes that's true. For rent control, it may well be true. Scrap it, more housing gets built, rents fall, and many tenants end up better off.

But it isn't true everywhere, automatically. And that's where the usual left-right fight gets stuck. One side says the efficiency gain is worth it. The other side says the equity loss is worth avoiding. They argue about where to set one knob: more redistribution and more waste, or less of both.
We're turning a different knob entirely.
Hold the amount of redistribution fixed. Exactly the same amount of help, going to exactly the same people. Now ask: can we deliver it with less waste?
Almost always, yes. And nobody loses their help.

We'll say it once more, for the people already drafting an angry comment. Same redistribution. Less waste. If you hear that as an argument for cutting welfare, you've just made the exact mistake this video is about.
lines.say: [deadpan] We'll say it once more, for the people already drafting an angry comment. Same redistribution. Less waste. If you hear that as an argument for cutting welfare, you've just made the exact mistake this video is about.

lines.text: Economics has a result for this, and it's been sitting in the textbooks for decades. The second welfare theorem.

In its ideal form, it says you can reach any distribution of resources you like, a little sharing or a lot, without shrinking the economy at all, as long as the money moves in ways that don't depend on what anyone does.
Real life never gets that perfect. But we can get much closer than any gift card ever will.
And this splits one fight into two. How much to share is a question of values. How to share is a question of engineering. And engineering has better and worse answers.
Start with taxes that don't block useful trades. There are two big ones.
Pollution first. When a factory dumps smoke on its neighbors for free, it produces too much, because someone else is paying part of the bill. Economists call that a negative externality.

A pollution tax hands the bill back to the polluter. And here's the remarkable part: this tax removes deadweight loss. The economy was producing too much smoke, and the tax pulls it back toward the right amount. The economist Arthur Pigou worked this out over a century ago, which is why these are called Pigouvian taxes. A tax that makes the pie bigger.
Next, land. Picture an empty lot. A train station opens nearby. Then shops, then a hospital, then thousands of neighbors. The lot is suddenly worth far more.
The owner didn't do any of that. The value soaked into the lot from everything around it. It's a positive externality, created by everyone else, captured by whoever holds the deed.

Now tax that land value. Look at who pays: the owner. Now look at who created the value: the train station, the shops, the hospital, the neighbors. The person paying the tax isn't the one whose work leaked into the land. And the bill is the same whether they build, sell, work, or sit in a lawn chair. Nothing they do changes it. No trade gets blocked. No deadweight loss.

How far can these two go? Further than most people think. Henry George argued in eighteen seventy-nine that a land tax alone could fund the government. And there's a good case that scrapping every other tax would push land values higher still, because much of what those taxes take would show up instead as higher land rents.

To the extent that still falls short, add one flat tax on consumption, with as few loopholes as possible. That part does block some trades. It shrinks the pie a little. So keep it as small as you can.
At this point someone always asks: but don't we want progressive taxes? Shouldn't the rich pay a bigger share?
Maybe. But first, which kind of progressive do you mean? Because there are two, and almost nobody separates them.
Your marginal tax rate is what you pay on the next dollar you earn. Your effective tax rate is what you pay overall, as a share of everything you earn.
Most people assume you need progressive marginal rates, higher brackets for higher incomes, to get progressive effective rates. You don't.

Watch. Take a flat forty percent tax. On income or on spending, the arithmetic works the same for anyone who spends what they earn, so let's use income to keep it simple. And give every citizen a ten-thousand-dollar dividend.
Earn twelve thousand dollars. You pay four thousand eight hundred in tax, get ten thousand back, and take home seventeen thousand two hundred. Your effective tax rate is negative forty-three percent.
Earn fifty thousand: an effective rate of twenty percent. A hundred thousand: thirty percent. A million: thirty-nine percent.
One marginal rate. Effective rates that climb from deeply negative to nearly forty percent. About as progressive as most bracket systems, with no brackets at all.
And the marginal rate is the one that matters for behavior, because it's what you face when you decide whether to take the extra shift. Which brings us to the ugliest number in the welfare state.

Here's what that looks like in practice. PolicyEngine, which builds an open-source model of the American tax and benefit system, ran the numbers for a single parent in California with two kids, paying rent and childcare on a low wage. Double their pay. After lost benefits, lost tax credits and higher taxes, the family keeps only about a fifth of the extra. An effective marginal tax rate of nearly eighty percent.

Read that again. A single parent near the poverty line can face a higher marginal tax rate than a billionaire. And at some incomes, losing a benefit all at once means earning more leaves you with less. That's the welfare cliff.
lines.say: [deadpan] Read that again. A single parent near the poverty line can face a higher marginal tax rate than a billionaire. And at some incomes, losing a benefit all at once means earning more leaves you with less. That's the welfare cliff.

lines.text: Remember the minimum wage fight? Under an eighty percent marginal rate, a worker keeps a fifth of every extra dollar. A fifteen-dollar minimum wage becomes a three-dollar one. People spend years fighting over the first number and never mention the second.
A flat dividend never shrinks when you earn more. No cliff. Every extra hour leaves you better off.

And notice what the check doesn't need. No means test. No caseworkers verifying your income every few months. No paperwork, no penalty for a good month. Means testing is what creates the cliffs in the first place, and it takes a bureaucracy to run. The dividend replaces that patchwork. Stack it on top of the old phase-outs, and you'd keep the cliffs.

And the old worry that handouts make people lazy? The Congressional Budget Office reviewed the research in twenty twelve. By its central estimates, people respond roughly five times more strongly to how much of the next dollar they get to keep than to simply having more money. So what kills the incentive to work is the high marginal rate built into means testing, far more than the cash itself.
Graduated brackets have a quieter problem. They punish uneven income. Take a simple system: ten percent on your first fifty thousand dollars, thirty percent on anything above that.

Earn fifty thousand this year and fifty thousand next year, and you pay ten thousand dollars in total. Earn a hundred thousand this year and nothing next year, the same money, and you pay twenty thousand. Twice the tax for the same two years of income.

Who earns like that? Freelancers. Farmers. Construction workers. Artists. Anyone who works double shifts one year and cares for a newborn the next. The bracket system charges them extra for the timing of their paychecks, which has nothing to do with how rich they are.
A flat rate with a dividend doesn't care. Earn it all in one year or spread it across two, and over the two years you pay exactly the same.
Which raises the obvious objection. Why should a millionaire get a ten-thousand-dollar check?

Because you can't look at the check by itself. You have to look at the taxes that pay for it. The millionaire gets ten thousand dollars and pays four hundred thousand. Most of any tax goes to everything else government does, so count only the share that pays for the checks: everyone above roughly average income pays in more than they get back, and everyone below gets back more than they pay. Net, it's a transfer from richer to poorer. The millionaire's check is just bookkeeping.

By the way, if you still object to rich people getting a check, then you should object far more to every price cap and every "don't you dare raise prices." A below-market price is a discount for every buyer, millionaires included, and there's no tax on the other side clawing it back from them. Same objection. Much worse offender.
lines.say: [dryly] By the way, if you still object to rich people getting a check, then you should object far more to every price cap and every "don't you dare raise prices." A below-market price is a discount for every buyer, millionaires included, and there's no tax on the other side clawing it back from them. Same objection. Much worse offender.

lines.text: Milton Friedman, not exactly a socialist, proposed something close to this in nineteen sixty-two. He called it a negative income tax: a payment that shrinks as you earn more. Set the rate it shrinks at equal to the flat tax rate, and it's mathematically the same as a dividend plus a flat tax. Make it shrink much faster than that, and you've rebuilt the cliff.
So, back to New York.
If the city wants delivery workers to have more money, it can give them money. Out in the open, where voters can see the price, paid for by taxes that don't block useful trades.
Instead it hides the bill inside every online order in the city. And when the bill arrives, the mayor calls it greed.
lines.say: [deadpan] Instead it hides the bill inside every online order in the city. And when the bill arrives, the mayor calls it greed.

lines.text: That's the socialist toolkit in one move. Good intentions, delivered by gift card, paid for by a tax nobody can see, and blamed on someone else.

So here's our challenge, to anyone who defends rent control because people deserve a home. Agreed, if that's your view. Now explain why you'd rather pin them to one apartment than give them the money to choose their own.
Pick any amount of redistribution you like. Zero, a little, a lot. Whatever it is, cash delivers it cheaper, and the people you meant to help end up with more.
There's an old name for this way of thinking, and it's been badly abused. Neoliberalism.

The word mostly gets thrown around as an insult, shorthand for austerity and deregulation. But it was coined in Paris in nineteen thirty-eight, at the Walter Lippmann Colloquium, by liberals who had watched laissez-faire collapse into the Depression, and watched communism and fascism rise in its place.

Their answer was a third road. Keep the market economy, because nothing else prices things so well or respects free choice. But give government real jobs: write the rules, correct the market's failures, and make sure nobody falls through. Even Friedrich Hayek, who founded the Mont Pelerin Society after the war, wrote that a basic minimum of food, shelter and clothing could be assured to everybody.

That's the tradition this video belongs to. A market economy and an open society. The freedom to love and marry whoever you choose. Cities covered in murals. Solar fields, wind turbines and nuclear plants powering all of it. And a safety net that treats people like adults: delivered in cash, without the waste.
Caring about the poor is the easy part. Doing the math is harder.
lines.say: [measured] Caring about the poor is the easy part. Doing the math is harder.

lines.text: Whatever you think people deserve, give it to them in cash.
